source_text: Celerum manente forma eius in suo ordine quantumlibet quaeras et tractes et omnem libidinem curiositatis effundas, si quid tibi videtur vel ambiguitate pendere vel obscuritate obumbrari. Est utique frater aliqui doctor gratia scientiae donatus, est aliqui inter exercitatos, conversatus aliqui tecum curiosus, tecum tamen quaerens novissime ignorare te melius sciet, ne quod non debeas noris, quia quod debeas nosti. Fides, inquit, tua te salvum fecit, non exercitatio scripturarum. Fides in regula posita est; habet legem et salutem de observatione legis: exercitatio autem in curiositate consistit, habens gloriam solam de peritiae studio. Cedat curiositas fidei, cedat gloria saluti. Certe aut non obstrepant, aut quiescant. Adversus regulam nihil scire omnia scire est. Ut non inimici essent veritatis haeretici, ut de refugiendis eis non praemoneremur, quale est conferre cum hominibus qui et ipsi adhuc se quaerere profiteantur? Si enim adhuc vere quaerunt, nihil adhuc certi repererunt, et ideo, quaecunque videntur interim tenere, dubitationem suam ostendunt, quamdiu quaerunt. Itaque tu, qui perinde quaeris, spectans ad eos qui et ipsi quaerunt, dubius ad dubios, incertus ad incertos, caecus a caecis in foveam deducaris necesse est. Sed cum decipiendi gratia praetendant se adhuc quaerere, ut nobis per sollicitudinis iniectionem tractatus suos insinuent, denique ubi adierunt ad nos, statim quae dicebant quaerenda esse defendant, iam illos sic debemus refutare, ut sciant nos non Christo, sed sibi negatores esse. Cum enim quaerunt adhuc, nondum tenet; cum autem non tenent, nondum crediderunt; cum autem nondum crediderunt, non sunt Christiani. At cum tenent quidem et credunt, quaerendum tamen dicunt, ut defendant. Antequam defendant, negant quod confitentur se nondum credidisse, dum quaerunt Qui ergo nec sibi sunt Christiani, quanto magis nobis? Qui per fallaciam veniunt, qualem fidem disputant? Cui veritati patrocinantur qui eam a mendacio inducunt? Sed ipsi de scripturis agunt, et de scripturis suadent! Aliunde scilicet loqui possent de rebus fidei, nisi ex litteris fidei?
thought_title: Faith, not curiosity, is the rule; heretics who still seek are not Christians
orientation: Tertullian has just stated the rule of faith and now argues that once the rule is held, there is nothing further to seek, and that heretics who claim still to be seeking thereby show they are not Christians.
pass_a_gloss: But while its form remains in its own order, however much you may seek and discuss and pour out every desire of curiosity, if anything seems to you either to hang in ambiguity or to be shadowed by obscurity. There is certainly some brother, a teacher gifted with the grace of knowledge; there is someone among the trained; someone curious has associated with you; yet seeking with you, he will know at last that you are better off not knowing, lest you know what you ought not, because you know what you ought. Faith, he says, has saved you, not exercise in the Scriptures. Faith is placed in the rule; it has law and salvation from the observance of the law: but exercise consists in curiosity, having glory alone from the zeal of skill. Let curiosity yield to faith, let glory yield to salvation. Certainly either let them not clamor, or let them be quiet. Against the rule to know nothing is to know everything. Even if heretics were not enemies of the truth, even if we were not warned beforehand to flee them, what sort of thing is it to confer with men who themselves still profess to be seeking? For if they still truly seek, they have found nothing certain as yet, and therefore, whatever they seem meanwhile to hold, they show their doubt, as long as they seek. And so you, who likewise seek, looking to those who themselves also seek, doubtful to the doubtful, uncertain to the uncertain, blind led by the blind, you must necessarily be led into the pit. But when for the sake of deceiving they pretend that they are still seeking, so that by the injection of anxiety they may insinuate their treatises to us, finally when they have come to us, they immediately defend the things which they were saying ought to be sought; now we ought to refute them in this way, so that they may know that we are deniers not of Christ, but of them. For when they still seek, they do not yet hold; but when they do not hold, they have not yet believed; but when they have not yet believed, they are not Christians. But when they do hold and believe, they nevertheless say that seeking must be done, in order to defend. Before they defend, they deny what they confess, that they had not yet believed, while they seek. Therefore those who are not Christians even to themselves, how much more to us? Those who come through deceit, what kind of faith do they dispute? What truth do they defend who introduce it from falsehood? But they themselves deal with the Scriptures, and they persuade from the Scriptures! Could they speak from elsewhere about the things of faith, except from the writings of faith?

choices.why: Keeps the contrast with faith as a settled possession; 'exercise' preserves the sense of practice or training rather than study.
Echoes the fixed term 'rule of faith' from the brief; here used absolutely for the same rule.
Preserves the jussive subjunctive force of the command.
Renders the passive sense of being led, matching the Gospel image Tertullian evokes.
Keeps the noun form and the pointed claim that rejecting heretics is not rejecting Christ.
Matches the brief's sense of heretical falsehood and the contrast with truth.

pass_b_english: But as long as the form of the rule remains in its proper order, you may seek and discuss as much as you like and pour out all the desire of your curiosity, if anything seems to you to hang in ambiguity or be shadowed by obscurity. There is certainly some brother endowed with the gift of knowledge, some one among the trained, some curious person who has spent time with you—yet one who seeks with you. In the end he will know better that you should be ignorant, so that you may not know what you ought not to know, because you know what you ought to know. "Your faith," he says, "has saved you," not your exercise in the Scriptures. Faith is placed in the rule; it has law and salvation from observing the law. Exercise, however, consists in curiosity, having glory only from the pursuit of skill. Let curiosity yield to faith; let glory yield to salvation. Certainly let them either not clamor against it, or be quiet. To know nothing against the rule is to know everything.

Even if heretics were not enemies of the truth, even if we were not warned beforehand to avoid them, what sort of thing is it to confer with people who themselves still profess to be seeking? For if they are still truly seeking, they have found nothing certain yet, and therefore whatever they seem to hold for the time being, they show their doubt as long as they seek. And so you, who likewise seek, looking to those who themselves seek, doubtful toward the doubtful, uncertain toward the uncertain, blind led by the blind, you must necessarily be led into the pit. But since they pretend to still be seeking for the sake of deceiving us, so that by injecting anxiety they may insinuate their arguments into us—indeed, when they come to us, they immediately defend the very things they said needed to be sought—we must refute them in such a way that they know we are deniers not of Christ, but of themselves. For when they are still seeking, they do not yet hold; and when they do not hold, they have not yet believed; and when they have not yet believed, they are not Christians. But when they do hold and believe, they nevertheless say that seeking is necessary, in order to defend. Before they defend, they deny what they confess—that they have not yet believed, while they seek. Therefore those who are not Christians even to themselves, how much more are they not Christians to us? By what faith do they dispute, who come through deceit? What truth do they plead for, who introduce it from falsehood? But they themselves argue from the Scriptures, and from the Scriptures they persuade! From where else, of course, could they speak about matters of faith, except from the writings of faith?
